sentences.text: Gryposuchus is an extinct genus of gavialid crocodilian, a group often described as hooked crocodiles.
This animal belongs to the class Reptilia and is classified within the family Gavialidae.
It is a member of the subfamily Gryposuchinae.
Based on orbital skeleton measurements, the species G. croizati is estimated to have reached a total length of 10.15 meters and a mass of approximately 1,745 kilograms.
The species name G. pachakamue references the Quechua term for a primordial god and narrator.
The type species Gryposuchus jessei was named in 1912 based on a well-preserved snout collected along the Pauini River in Brazil.
Unfortunately, the holotype specimen of G. jessei was likely destroyed in 1943 during the bombing of Hamburg in World War II.
Cranial materials from the Pebas Formation in Iquitos, Peru, were named Gryposuchus pachakamue in 2016 by Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and colleagues.
A fossil consisting of a premaxilla and a maxilla was discovered in 1997 at the Sena Madureia site in the Late Miocene Solimões Formation.

The species G. neogaeus was included in the genus in 1982, though its specimens were originally described in 1885 from the Late Miocene Ituzaingó Formation in Argentina and referred to Rhamphostomopsis at the time.
The species G. colombianus was named in 1965 from Middle Miocene deposits in Colombia and Late Miocene formations in Venezuela, and was originally referred to the modern genus Gavialis.

The species G. croizati, described in 2009, was found in the Urumaco Formation in northeastern Venezuela and is distinguished by a reduced number of maxillary teeth, a thin interfenestral parietal bar, and a widely separated and reduced palatal fenestra.

Gryposuchus was likely the most successful gryposuchine in South America because it was adapted to freshwater environments, unlike many related species that lived in estuarine, coastal, or marine waters.
Although Gryposuchus reached Argentina by the Middle Miocene, known species diversity peaked in the Late Miocene with four to five species present, three of which coexisted in the Urumaco Formation.

G. pachakamue is characterized by having 22 teeth in both the jaw and maxilla, a snout length comparable to the modern Gavialis gangeticus, and eye orbits that were wider than long and less rotated upward than in other gavialids, implying it lacked fully developed telescopic eyes.

The aridification of the continental interior and the filling of wetland basins likely caused the extinction of Gryposuchus by restricting space and food resources for these large, specialized crocodilians.
Gryposuchus is the type genus of the subfamily Gryposuchinae, though a 2018 study suggests this group might be paraphyletic and represents an evolutionary grade leading to the gharial.
A 2007 phylogenetic analysis placed Gryposuchus within the subfamily Gryposuchinae alongside the genera Aktiogavialis, Ikanogavialis, Piscogavialis, and Siquisiquesuchus.
The genus Gryposuchus was named by Gürich in 1912.
Gryposuchus lived during the Miocene epoch, specifically from the Colhuehuapian to the Huayquerian ages.
The time range for Gryposuchus spans from the Burdigalian to the Late Pleistocene, approximately 20.45 to 0.0117 million years ago.
Fossils of Gryposuchus have been found in Argentina, Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil, and the Peruvian Amazon.

G. pachakamue inhabited the proto-Amazonian river system 13 million years ago and represents the oldest record of gavialids in that area, suggesting its primitive telescopic eye condition evolved convergently with Asian Gavialis species.

The extinction of Gavialoidea and Crocodyloidea in South America was likely caused by the continued uplift of the northern Andes, which redirected Caribbean river mouths to the colder Atlantic and transformed hyperdiverse crocodilian wetlands into a fully developed river delta system.
At the Miocene/Pliocene boundary, all Gavialoidea and Crocodyloidea were likely extirpated from South America.
It is debated whether G. neogaeus and G. colombianus are synonyms of G. jessei, but most researchers consider them distinct species due to significant anatomical differences.
